name: Shor's Factoring Algorithm
subject: quantum-computing
subjectTitle: A Skeptic's Guide to Quantum Computing

lesson.title: The Algorithm That Made Cryptographers Nervous
lesson.summary: Shor's algorithm shows that a large enough quantum computer could factor huge numbers exponentially faster than any known classical method, which is exactly why RSA encryption is considered at risk.
lesson.body:
Most of the theoretical promise of quantum computing, the idea that a quantum computer could solve certain problems dramatically faster than any classical machine, traces back to one 1994 result: Peter Shor's algorithm for factoring large integers. Factoring, breaking a number down into its prime building blocks, is easy for small numbers and brutally hard for large ones on a classical computer. The best known classical factoring methods scale roughly exponentially with the size of the number, which is precisely why RSA encryption, the backbone of a huge amount of internet security, is built on numbers with hundreds of digits: factoring them classically would take longer than the age of the universe with any foreseeable classical hardware.

Shor's insight was to reframe factoring as a different problem entirely: finding the period of a repeating mathematical pattern. If you repeatedly compute a number raised to increasing powers modulo a large composite number, the results eventually cycle, and that cycle length, the period, turns out to reveal the number's prime factors through a bit of classical number theory once you know it. Finding that period classically is itself hard, but a quantum computer can prepare a superposition over many possible inputs at once and then apply a quantum Fourier transform, a quantum analog of the classical Fourier transform used to detect frequencies in a signal, to make the periodic structure interfere constructively at the correct answer and destructively everywhere else. The period pops out of a measurement with high probability, and ordinary classical math finishes the job from there.

This is why Shor's algorithm is such a big deal: it does not offer a modest speedup, it offers an exponential one, turning a problem that is intractable classically into one that is efficient on a sufficiently capable quantum computer. That gap is the entire reason cryptographers, standards bodies, and governments have spent the past decade developing and migrating toward post quantum cryptographic schemes built on different mathematical problems that Shor's method does not help with.

The catch, and it is a large one given everything covered in this chapter on hardware, is what "sufficiently capable" means in practice. Running Shor's algorithm on a cryptographically relevant number, something the size used in RSA-2048, requires not just many physical qubits but many stable, error corrected logical qubits sustained through a long, precise circuit. One widely cited 2019 estimate put the physical qubit requirement, given realistic error rates and error correction overhead, in the tens of millions, several orders of magnitude beyond any hardware that exists today on any of the five platforms just discussed. Current experiments have factored small numbers like 15 and 21 using simplified or partially compiled circuits, which demonstrates the principle but says very little about when, or whether, a machine capable of threatening real encryption will actually be built.
